concept.name: Treasury bond
concept.definition: A long-term U.S. Treasury marketable security — historically a 30-year investment and now offered in 20-year terms as well — that pays interest every six months and is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government.
concept.intuition: A Treasury bond is the longest-term loan to the U.S. government: decades of fixed semiannual coupons, which makes its price the most rate-sensitive of the marketable Treasuries.
concept.mechanics: Bonds are auctioned, pay fixed semiannual coupons, and mature at 20 or 30 years. Their long duration means small yield moves produce large price swings; the long end of the Treasury curve anchors pension discount rates, mortgage pricing, and term-premium analysis.
concept.failure_modes: Long duration amplifies interest-rate risk — a 100 basis point rise in yields can erase roughly a fifth of a 30-year bond's market value. Over long horizons, inflation is the dominant real-return risk.
concept.misconceptions: That Treasury bonds are the same as U.S. savings bonds — savings bonds are non-marketable retail products that cannot be sold or transferred, while Treasury bonds are marketable securities. Also, 'full faith and credit' does not protect the market price before maturity.
concept.example: A 30-year Treasury bond bought at par with a 4.5% coupon pays $22.50 per $1,000 face every six months until 2055, when the principal is returned.
